description: Cross-domain linkage snapshot for Faultline. Records come from four analyst-coded platform datasets. Links are derived only from fields present in those datasets, through the crosswalk tables included here.

nuclear.name: Global Nuclear Infrastructure Atlas
files: src/data/enrichedFacilities.js (digital I&C and cyber overlay fields)

tiers.same-event: The same incident is recorded in both datasets: same name and year, a cited source naming both (relatedRecords), or the same named target in the same year.
tiers.same-intrusion-set: The records list the same MITRE ATT&CK group (intrusionSetIds); without IDs, a cyber alias appears in the orbital actor field. They may be different operations by the same group.

tierRule: A link is same-event when one of its bases is same_event; otherwise it is same-intrusion-set. Shared states and infrastructure categories are reported as facets, not links.
facetRule: A facet lists a state or infrastructure category that records in two or more datasets connect to, with the records and their role in each dataset (actor, target, host, profiled, category). It says the datasets both include the entity, not that the records are related.

basisTypes.same_event: Same incident recorded in two datasets
basisTypes.same_intrusion_set: Same intrusion set named in both records
basisTypes.attributed_state: Record names this state as the acting state
basisTypes.target_state: Record names this state as a target
basisTypes.host_state: Record is located in this state
basisTypes.profiled_state: State profiled in lunar data (a country authority profile, not an actor in an event)
basisTypes.infrastructure_category: Record falls in this shared infrastructure category (see crosswalk)

crosswalks.stateRule: A field is linked to a state only when its value, with any parenthetical removed and split on '/', matches a listed spelling exactly. Values such as 'Unknown', 'Multiple', 'Global' or 'Central Europe' are not linked. An actor field is not linked when a parenthetical says the actor is criminal, not the state, individuals or similar, or when the record's attribution confidence is below high.

rules.match: every commercial nuclear power plant record
text contains: communication, satellite internet, broadband, Starlink, KA-SAT, SATCOM
type is spoofing, or subtype or target text contains GNSS or GPS

crosswalks.instrumentRule: Instrument strings are mapped to a canonical instrument when they match a listed pattern or source id. Unmatched strings keep their own instrument node.

nodes.label: Torness Nuclear Power Station
nodes.summary: Two-unit AGR station on the Scottish coast; one of Scotland's two nuclear stations.

fields.safeguardsStatus: Voluntary Offer Agreement (VOA) - NPT Weapon State

nodes.label: Hinkley Point C
nodes.summary: Two-unit EPR plant under construction in Somerset. First new UK nuclear station in decades; expected online mid-2020s. Subject to significant cost and schedule revisions.

fields.safeguardsStatus: Voluntary Offer Agreement (VOA) - NPT Weapon State

nodes.label: Sendai Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: First Japanese plant to restart after post-Fukushima new regulatory framework (2015). Two Mitsubishi PWR units in Kagoshima Prefecture.

nodes.label: Genkai Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two active units restarted under NRA post-Fukushima safety framework. Units 1–2 permanently shutdown.

nodes.label: Takahama Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Four-unit PWR in Fukui Prefecture. Units 3–4 have restarted; Units 1–2 among first old plants approved for 60-year operation.

nodes.label: Fukushima Daini Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Fukushima Daini (No. 2) plant, 12 km south of Fukushima Daiichi. All 4 units permanently shut down; decommissioning decided in 2019.

nodes.label: Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two operating VVER-1000 units (Russian design) in Tamil Nadu. Additional units under construction. India's largest single nuclear station.

nodes.label: Tarapur Atomic Power Station
nodes.summary: India's first commercial nuclear station. Units 1–2 are original GE BWRs (1969); Units 3–4 are PHWR designs.

nodes.label: Rajasthan Atomic Power Station
nodes.summary: Six PHWR units in Rajasthan. India's nuclear programme uses domestically evolved PHWR technology derived from early Canadian CANDU collaboration.

nodes.label: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Europe's largest nuclear station. All six units in cold shutdown since 2022 due to conflict conditions. IAEA expert presence maintained. Publicly documented through regular IAEA reports.

nodes.label: Rivne Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Four-unit mixed VVER station in western Ukraine. Operating as of latest public reporting.

nodes.label: South Ukraine Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Three-unit VVER-1000 station in Mykolaiv Oblast. Operating as of latest public reporting.

nodes.label: Olkiluoto Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: OL3 (EPR, 1600 MWe) began commercial operation April 2023 — first new reactor in Western Europe in ~16 years and world's most powerful single reactor unit.

nodes.label: Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two VVER-440 units on the Gulf of Finland coast. Finnish-modified Soviet design with western safety upgrades.

nodes.label: Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Three-unit ABB BWR station in Uppsala County. One of Europe's most efficient nuclear stations.

nodes.label: Ringhals Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two units operating (Ringhals 3 and 4, PWR). Units 1 and 2 permanently shut 2019–2020.

nodes.label: Doel Nuclear Power Station
nodes.summary: Three active PWR units near Antwerp. Belgium decided to extend Doel 4 operation to 2035 and pursue lifetime extension for Doel 3.

nodes.label: Tihange Nuclear Power Station
nodes.summary: Two operating PWR units on the Meuse River. Belgium extended Tihange 3 to 2035; Tihange 1–2 operational life decisions ongoing.

nodes.label: Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Four VVER-440 units, significantly modernised. ČEZ planning new unit construction adjacent to existing site.

nodes.label: Temelín Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two VVER-1000 units with Western instrumentation and control systems. South Bohemia.

nodes.label: Paks Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Four VVER-440 units supplying ~50% of Hungary's electricity. Life extension approved. Paks II (new units) in planning/permitting.

nodes.label: Almaraz Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Spain's largest nuclear station. Operational life extended; scheduled shutdown under Spain's national energy plan.

nodes.label: Cofrentes Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Spain's only BWR. Single-unit GE BWR in Valencia region.

nodes.label: Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Switzerland's newest and most powerful nuclear station. Single-unit GE BWR.

nodes.label: Beznau Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: World's oldest operating commercial nuclear power plant (Unit 1 since 1969). Two Westinghouse PWR units.

nodes.label: Isar 2 (Kernkraftwerk Isar 2)
nodes.summary: Permanently shut 15 April 2023 — one of the last three German nuclear plants to close under Germany's Atomausstieg (nuclear phase-out) policy.

nodes.label: Borssele Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Netherlands' only operating nuclear station. Lifetime extended. Government planning at least two new large reactors.

nodes.label: Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant
nodes.summary: First nuclear power plant in the Arab world. Four APR-1400 units. Units 1–3 in commercial operation; Unit 4 commissioning. Developed with Korean technology by KEPCO.

nodes.label: Atucha Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Argentina's flagship nuclear site. Atucha I (1974) was Latin America's first commercial nuclear plant. Atucha II joined commercial operation in 2014.

nodes.label: Angra Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two PWR units in Rio de Janeiro State. Angra 3 under construction (delayed). Brazil's only commercial nuclear station.

nodes.label: Koeberg Nuclear Power Station
nodes.summary: Africa's only commercial nuclear power station. Two French Framatome PWR units north of Cape Town. 20-year life extension approved.

nodes.label: Karachi Nuclear Power Plant (KANUPP)
nodes.summary: Pakistan's primary civilian nuclear station. KANUPP-1 (1971, now shutdown). KANUPP-2 and KANUPP-3 (Hualong One, Chinese-supplied) in operation as of 2021–2022.

nodes.label: Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Iran's only commercial nuclear power plant. VVER-1000 built with Russian assistance. Unit 2 under construction. Operates under IAEA safeguards.

fields.safeguardsStatus: CSA (INFCIRC/214) - Additional Protocol signed but not ratified

nodes.label: Laguna Verde Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Mexico's only nuclear plant. Two GE BWR units in Veracruz. Provides ~4% of Mexico's electricity.

nodes.label: Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Two CANDU-6 units on the Danube. Provides ~20% of Romania's electricity. Units 3–5 in long-term planning.

nodes.label: Krško Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Jointly owned and operated by Slovenia and Croatia. Single Westinghouse PWR supplying both national grids.

nodes.label: Armenian Nuclear Power Plant (Metsamor)
nodes.summary: One of the older VVER-440 designs still in operation. Provides a significant share of Armenia's electricity. Life extension underway.

nodes.label: Ostrovets Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Belarus's first and only nuclear power plant. Two VVER-1200 units built by Rosatom. Unit 1 in commercial operation since 2021; Unit 2 from 2023.

nodes.label: Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant, built with Russian assistance. Two VVER-1200 units. Expected to begin operation in the 2020s.

nodes.label: Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Turkey's first nuclear plant, built on a BOO (Build-Own-Operate) model by Rosatom. Four VVER-1200 units. Construction ongoing.

nodes.label: El-Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant
nodes.summary: Egypt's first nuclear plant, four VVER-1200 units. Construction underway on the Mediterranean coast.

nodes.label: Due Regard (Outer Space Treaty)
nodes.summary: No external arbiter determines what constitutes "due regard." Each spacefaring state defines the threshold of consideration owed to others, creating asymmetric obligation based on capability.

nodes.label: Harmful Interference (Artemis Accords)
nodes.summary: Sets the boundary for deconfliction without a central judge. The drafting party retains interpretive control over what constitutes "harmful" activity near its operations.

nodes.label: Safety Zone (Artemis Accords)
nodes.summary: Functional exclusion zones without treaty basis. The "notifying" state defines the perimeter, converting operational presence into territorial-adjacent authority.

nodes.label: Co-consultation (Roscosmos–CNSA Memorandum of Understanding on the ILRS)
nodes.summary: Consultation without voting rights. Joining partners are consulted but founding states retain architectural control over station design, location, and operational rules.

fields.document: Roscosmos–CNSA Memorandum of Understanding on the ILRS

nodes.label: Appropriate Utilization (ILRS Guide for Partnership)
nodes.summary: Resource use framed as "appropriate" without defining limits, allowing the lead agency to set extraction norms through precedent rather than negotiation.

nodes.label: National Interest (UAE Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 on the Regulation of the Space Sector)
nodes.summary: Data sharing obligations yield to undefined "national interest," creating a black-box override for transparency commitments.

fields.document: UAE Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 on the Regulation of the Space Sector

nodes.label: Peaceful Purposes (Japan Basic Space Law)
nodes.summary: Shift from "non-military" to "non-aggressive" interpretation. The executive branch claimed authority to redefine a constitutional constraint without legislative amendment.

nodes.label: Appropriation (negative definition) (Luxembourg Space Resources Law)
nodes.summary: Defines what appropriation is NOT (national sovereignty claim) to permit what it IS (commercial extraction). Reframes OST Article II through silence on resource rights.

nodes.label: Centralized Authorization (India Space Activities Bill)
nodes.summary: Single gateway authorization concentrates interpretive authority over all commercial and international space activity involving Indian entities.

fields.holder: IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre)

nodes.label: Lunar Time Standard (OSTP Coordinated Lunar Time (LTC) Framework)
nodes.summary: Authority over reference frames. Whoever defines the time standard for cislunar space defines the coordination infrastructure all actors must adopt.

nodes.label: Multilateral Alignment (ESA Statement on Artemis Accords Principles)
nodes.summary: Defers to existing multilateral frameworks (COPUOS) while participating operationally in Artemis, creating dual-track legitimation.

fields.document: ESA Statement on Artemis Accords Principles

nodes.label: Phase 4 Exploration (CNSA Lunar Exploration Programme Phase 4)
nodes.summary: Phased programme structure allows iterative expansion of scope without requiring partner re-consent at each stage. Architectural decisions cascade.

nodes.label: As Appropriate (Artemis Accords)
nodes.summary: "As appropriate" delegates implementation entirely to the signatory. No external standard defines what is or is not appropriate, allowing each actor to calibrate compliance to their own interests.

nodes.label: Non-military / Non-aggressive (Japan Basic Space Law + JAXA-NASA Artemis MoU (Gateway / HLS))
nodes.summary: Japan reserves the interpretation of "peaceful use" to domestic law. The shift from "non-military" to "non-aggressive" enables dual-use space capabilities under constitutional cover.

fields.document: Japan Basic Space Law + JAXA-NASA Artemis MoU (Gateway / HLS)

nodes.label: Authorised Entity (India Space Activities Bill)
nodes.summary: The criteria for "authorised entity" status are not defined in statute, vesting complete discretion in the Central Government to approve or reject any actor entering the space sector.

nodes.label: Interoperability Standards (ESA Statement on Artemis Accords Principles + LunaNet Interoperability Specification)
nodes.summary: ESA advocates for multilateral standard-setting but depends on NASA-defined LunaNet interoperability standards. De jure multilateralism coexists with de facto US technical authority.

fields.document: ESA Statement on Artemis Accords Principles + LunaNet Interoperability Specification
fields.holder: NASA (de facto) / ESA (de jure multilateral claim)

nodes.label: Ownership vs. Appropriation (Luxembourg Space Resources Law + U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act)
nodes.summary: The boundary between "ownership of extracted resources" (permitted) and "appropriation of celestial bodies" (prohibited by OST) is drawn unilaterally by national legislation without international adjudication.

fields.document: Luxembourg Space Resources Law + U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act

nodes.label: United States lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: Defines safety zones, time standards, and interoperability requirements that all partners must adopt.

nodes.label: China lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: CNSA controls station architecture, phase definitions, and partner onboarding criteria.

nodes.label: Russia lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: Co-founding status grants architectural veto and privileged consultation not available to later joiners.

documents: Roscosmos–CNSA Memorandum of Understanding on the ILRS

nodes.label: Japan lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: Cabinet Office holds interpretive monopoly over what "peaceful" means in practice, enabling progressive militarization.

nodes.label: India lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: IN-SPACe holds exclusive authorization power over all commercial and international space activity by Indian entities.

nodes.label: Luxembourg lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: Unilaterally defines what "appropriation" is NOT, permitting commercial extraction without multilateral consent.

nodes.label: United Arab Emirates lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: "National interest" override allows selective opacity despite formal transparency commitments.

documents: UAE Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 on the Regulation of the Space Sector

nodes.label: ESA / European Union lunar authority profile
nodes.summary: Defers authority to "future multilateral norms" while locking in operational participation now — the norms will have to accommodate the facts.

documents: ESA Statement on Artemis Accords Principles

nodes.label: Navigation: NASA / OSTP
nodes.summary: Defining Coordinated Lunar Time (LTC) creates a reference frame all cislunar actors must synchronize to. Operational necessity becomes normative infrastructure.

nodes.label: Communications: NASA (LunaNet)
nodes.summary: Relay network architecture determines who can communicate, when, and through what protocols. Network access = operational permission.

nodes.label: Power Systems: CNSA (ILRS Phase 4)
nodes.summary: Nuclear fission power plant at lunar south pole creates dependency. Power sharing agreements become governance instruments.

fields.example: ILRS nuclear power plant for south pole base

nodes.label: In-Situ Resource Utilization: Multiple (contested)
nodes.summary: First extraction creates operational precedent. "Safety zones" around extraction sites convert resource use into spatial authority.

fields.example: Artemis Accords Section 11 + Luxembourg Space Resources Law

nodes.label: Space Situational Awareness: US Space Command / 18th SDS
nodes.summary: Comprehensive tracking capability creates information asymmetry. The actor who "sees" the space environment defines what constitutes risk.

fields.example: Space fence radar + cislunar domain awareness expansion

nodes.label: Habitats: CNSA / Roscosmos (ILRS)
nodes.summary: Permanent presence converts occupancy into operational authority. Habitat location choices pre-empt future resource access by establishing "prior use."

fields.example: ILRS south pole base site selection

nodes.label: Logistics: NASA (Gateway + HLS)
nodes.summary: Controlling the logistics chain (orbital station, lander, surface transport) determines who can reach the lunar surface and when.

fields.example: Lunar Gateway as staging point + HLS contract structure

limitations: All four source datasets are analyst-coded from public sources. Coding choices in those datasets carry into this layer.
The datasets are not exhaustive. A missing link means no link can be derived from the coded fields, not that no relationship exists.
Facets (a state or infrastructure category present in two datasets) show co-occurrence in the data, not causation, coordination or a relationship between the records.
The cyber atlas lists target sectors and target countries separately, so a case that lists energy and Germany does not say it targeted the German energy sector.

Instrument references show which instruments each dataset associates with a record. Orbital incident and nuclear plant records reference no instrument at record level, so instrument coverage reflects the schema of each dataset, not a legal conclusion that no law applies.
Free-text fields (summaries, policy responses) are not parsed for links, except the short keyword rules listed in the sector crosswalk.
This layer describes recorded events. It makes no prediction.
